cards.title: Harriet Tubman
read: Harriet Tubman was born around 1822 in Maryland. She was enslaved, which means she was not free. In 1849 she made a brave choice: she walked north and found her freedom.
Harriet wanted her family and friends to be free too. She went back about 13 times to guide them on the Underground Railroad. It was not a train. It was a secret path of safe houses and kind helpers.
Harriet was clever and careful. She traveled at night and used the North Star to find her way. Later she lived in Auburn, New York, where she opened her home to people who needed care.
facts: She guided about 70 people to freedom.
She said she never lost a passenger.
In the Civil War she worked as a nurse, a scout and a spy.
She helped lead a mission that freed more than 700 people.
She loved to sing, and stories say she sometimes used songs as secret signals.
words: being able to choose how you live
owned by another person and forced to work without pay
a secret path of people who helped others escape to freedom
questions: Where was Harriet Tubman born?
What was the Underground Railroad?
What helped Harriet find her way at night?

cards.title: Mae Jemison
read: Mae Jemison was born in 1956 in Alabama and grew up in Chicago. As a girl she loved science, space and dance.
Mae became a doctor and an engineer. Then she became an astronaut. In 1992 she flew on the Space Shuttle Endeavour. She was the first African American woman to go to space.
Mae took a poster of a dancer and other special things with her into space. Later she started a science camp for kids. She wants every child to keep asking questions about the world.
facts: Her space trip lasted about 8 days.
She did science tests in space.
Before space, she was a Peace Corps doctor in West Africa.
She started college at age 16.
In space, the shuttle circled Earth in orbit.
words: a person trained to travel in space
a person who designs and builds things
the path something takes around a planet
questions: What did Mae Jemison love as a girl?
What year did she go to space?
Name two jobs she had.

cards.title: The Wright Brothers
read: Wilbur and Orville Wright were brothers from Dayton, Ohio. They ran a bicycle shop. They also dreamed about flying.

They built gliders and tested them again and again. On December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, they made the first flight of an airplane with an engine. Orville was the pilot, and he flew for 12 seconds.
The brothers studied how birds turn their wings. They used that idea to steer their plane. A few years later they built planes that could fly for more than an hour.
facts: The first flight went 120 feet, about the length of 3 school buses.
They flew 4 times that day.
The longest flight that day lasted 59 seconds.
They used ideas from fixing bicycles.
Their airplane is in a museum in Washington, D.C.
words: a plane with no engine that floats on the wind
a machine that makes something move
the person who flies a plane
questions: What kind of shop did the brothers run?
Where did they fly the first airplane?
How long was the first flight?

cards.title: Jackie Robinson
read: Jackie Robinson was born in 1919 in Georgia and grew up in California. In college he played four sports: baseball, football, basketball and track.

Before 1947, Black players had been kept out of the major leagues, which was unfair. That year Jackie joined the Brooklyn Dodgers and changed baseball for good. Some people were unkind to him, but Jackie showed courage and played great baseball.
Jackie was fast and loved to steal bases, even home plate! He helped the Dodgers win the World Series in 1955. After baseball, he worked to make life fairer for everyone.
facts: He was Rookie of the Year in 1947.
He wore number 42.
Every Major League team stopped giving out number 42 to new players, to honor him.
Every April 15 is Jackie Robinson Day, when every player wears 42 to honor him.
He helped open the door for many players.
words: a group of teams that play each other
a player in the first year
being brave when something is hard
questions: What team did Jackie Robinson join in 1947?
What number did he wear?
What happens every April 15?

cards.title: The Grand Canyon
read: The Grand Canyon is a giant, deep valley in Arizona. The Colorado River runs along the bottom.
Over millions of years, the river cut through the rock little by little. Now you can see layers of red, orange and tan rock, like stripes in a cake. The oldest layers are at the bottom.
Rangers lead hikes and tell stories about the rocks, plants and animals. Condors, some of the biggest birds in North America, fly over the canyon. At sunset the rocks seem to glow red and gold.
facts: It is about 277 miles long.
At its deepest, it is more than a mile deep.
It became a national park in 1919.
Native American nations, like the Havasupai and the Hualapai, have lived in and near the canyon for a very long time, and they still do.
Millions of people visit every year.
words: a deep valley with steep sides
a long stream of moving water
one flat part on top of another
questions: What state is the Grand Canyon in?
What river made the canyon?
Where are the oldest rock layers?

cards.title: Antarctica
read: Antarctica is a continent at the bottom of the world. The South Pole is there. It is the coldest, windiest and driest continent on Earth.
Almost all of Antarctica is covered by thick ice. No one lives there all year as a home. Scientists and workers stay for a while to study the ice, the weather and the animals.

Emperor penguins huddle close together to stay warm in winter storms. Scientists drill deep into the ice to learn about Earth long ago. Many countries agreed to keep Antarctica a place for peace and science.
facts: The ice is more than a mile thick in many places.
Penguins and seals live on the coast.
Most of Earth's fresh water is frozen there.
In winter the sun does not rise for weeks or months in many places.
The coldest air ever measured was there.
words: one of Earth's seven big pieces of land
a huge layer of ice that covers land
a person who studies the world to learn how it works
questions: What is Antarctica covered by?
Who stays in Antarctica, and why?
Name one animal that lives there.

cards.title: The Amazon Rainforest
read: The Amazon is the biggest rainforest in the world. It is in South America, and most of it is in Brazil. It rains a lot there.
The Amazon River winds through the forest. Tall trees make a roof of leaves called the canopy. Millions of kinds of plants, insects and animals live there. So do many Indigenous peoples.
Some trees in the Amazon are taller than a 15-story building. Pink river dolphins swim in its rivers. The forest makes clouds and rain that help water much of South America.
facts: The Amazon reaches into 9 countries and territories, like Brazil, Peru and Colombia.
Sloths, jaguars and toucans live there.
The Amazon River carries more water than any other river.
Many medicines come from rainforest plants.
It is warm all year.
words: a thick forest where it rains a lot
the roof of leaves at the top of a forest
people whose families have lived in a place since long before others came
questions: What continent is the Amazon on?
What is the canopy?
Name two animals that live in the Amazon.

cards.title: The Great Barrier Reef
read: The Great Barrier Reef is in the ocean near Australia. It is the biggest coral reef system in the world. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have cared for this sea for a very long time.
Coral looks like rock or plants, but it is made of tiny animals. They build hard homes that grow into reefs over many years. Fish, sea turtles and sharks find food and shelter there.
Clownfish hide in the stinging arms of sea anemones, where they are safe. Sea turtles swim back to the same beaches to lay their eggs. People work hard to keep the reef clean and healthy.
facts: It is made of about 3,000 reefs.
It is about 1,400 miles long.
Astronauts can see parts of it from space.
More than 1,500 kinds of fish live there.
Warm water can make coral sick and turn white.
words: tiny sea animals that build hard homes
a long ridge of coral or rock under the sea
questions: What country is the reef near?
What is coral made of?
Name two animals that live on the reef.

cards.title: The Moon
read: The Moon moves around Earth. It takes about a month to go all the way around. The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because sunlight bounces off it.
As the Moon moves, we see different amounts of its sunny side. These shapes are called phases. In 1969, astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon.
The Moon has no air, so astronauts wore space suits to breathe. They brought back Moon rocks for scientists to study. The Moon's pull helps make the ocean tides go up and down.
facts: The Moon is about 239,000 miles away.
Twelve astronauts have walked on it.
It is covered with holes called craters.
You would weigh much less on the Moon.
Footprints there can last a very long time, because there is no wind or rain.
words: the path something takes around another thing
a round hole made when a space rock hits
the shape of the lit part of the Moon we see
questions: Why does the Moon shine?
What are the Moon's shapes called?
Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?

cards.title: Volcanoes
read: Deep under the ground, it is so hot that rock melts. This melted rock is called magma. A volcano is an opening where magma can come up.
When a volcano erupts, the melted rock pours out. Then it is called lava. When lava cools, it turns into new rock. Some islands, like Hawaii, were built by volcanoes.

Volcano ash can make the soil very rich, so plants grow well near some volcanoes. Scientists watch volcanoes with special tools to help warn people when an eruption may be coming. Some volcanoes are on other planets too, like Mars.
facts: There are volcanoes on land and under the sea.
Lava can be hotter than an oven.
Some volcanoes are quiet for many years.
Mauna Loa in Hawaii is one of the biggest volcanoes on Earth.
Scientists who study volcanoes are called volcanologists.
words: melted rock that has come out of the ground
questions: What is magma?
What is melted rock called when it comes out?
Name a place that volcanoes built.

cards.title: Rainbows
read: Sunlight looks white, but it is really made of many colors mixed together. When sunlight shines into raindrops, the drops bend the light and split it into its colors.
To see a rainbow, stand with the sun behind you and the rain in front of you. The colors always come in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.
Rainbows often show up after a storm, when the sun comes out again. You may also see one in the spray of a waterfall. Each raindrop acts like a tiny prism that splits the light.
facts: A rainbow is really a circle. From the ground we see only part.
Sometimes you can see two rainbows at once.
In a double rainbow, the colors of the second one are flipped.
You can make a rainbow with a garden hose on a sunny day.
Red is at the top, on the outside edge.
words: what lets us see; it comes from the sun and lamps
to turn from a straight line
questions: What is sunlight really made of?
Where should the sun be when you look for a rainbow?
What color is at the top of a rainbow?

cards.title: Bicycles
read: A bicycle has two wheels, a seat, handlebars and pedals. When you push the pedals, a chain turns the back wheel, and the bike rolls forward.
The first bike was made in 1817 in Germany. It had no pedals at all. Riders pushed it along with their feet, like a balance bike.
Bike tires are filled with air, which makes the ride softer. Gears help riders climb hills more easily. Some people ride bikes all the way across a country!
facts: There are about a billion bikes in the world.
Bikes do not need gas to go.
Riding is great exercise for your heart and legs.
Always wear a helmet when you ride. It protects your head if you fall.
Some bikes are built for two riders.
words: the part you push with your foot
metal links that turn the wheel
questions: What turns the back wheel?
What was missing from the first bike?
Why should you wear a helmet?

cards.title: Octopus
read: An octopus lives in the ocean. It has eight arms covered with suckers. The suckers can grab, feel and even taste.

An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through tiny spaces. To hide, it uses camouflage. It changes its color and even the bumps on its skin. If a hungry fish comes close, it can squirt a cloud of ink and swim away.
Some baby octopuses are smaller than a grain of rice when they hatch. Octopuses are curious and like to explore. Some have learned to open jars to get food inside.
facts: An octopus has three hearts.
Its blood is blue.
It is very smart and can solve puzzles.
It eats crabs, clams and fish.
Some octopuses carry shells to hide in.
words: a round cup that sticks to things
colors or shapes that help an animal hide
a dark liquid an octopus squirts to escape
questions: How many arms does an octopus have?
Name one way an octopus hides.
How many hearts does it have?

cards.title: Honeybee
read: Honeybees live together in a home called a hive. One hive can have thousands of bees. There is one queen, who lays the eggs. Worker bees do most of the other jobs.

Worker bees fly to flowers and drink a sweet juice called nectar. Back at the hive, they turn nectar into honey. As they visit flowers, they carry pollen from one flower to the next, which helps plants make seeds and fruit.

Bees keep the hive warm in winter by huddling close and shivering their wing muscles. One worker bee makes only a tiny bit of honey in its whole life. It takes many bees working together to fill a jar.
facts: Bees do a waggle dance to show other bees where flowers are.
A bee has five eyes.
Bees help grow many foods we eat, like apples.
Wax for the hive comes from the bees' bodies.
A bee buzzes because its wings beat very fast.
words: the home where a big group of bees lives
a tiny, dusty powder that plants need to make seeds
questions: Who lays the eggs in a hive?
What do bees make honey from?
How do bees help plants?

cards.title: Polar Bear
read: Polar bears live in the Arctic, the cold land and sea near the North Pole. They spend much of their lives on sea ice and hunt seals.
A polar bear's fur looks white, but each hair is really clear. Under the fur, its skin is black, which helps soak up the sun's warmth. A thick layer of fat keeps it warm too.
A polar bear can smell a seal from far away, even under the snow. Mother bears stay in their dens with their cubs for months. In spring the cubs come out and learn to hunt.
facts: Polar bears are great swimmers.
A big male can weigh more than 1,000 pounds.
Their big paws help them walk on ice and paddle in water.
Cubs are born in a snow den.
They need sea ice to hunt.
words: the cold area around the North Pole
an animal that hunts other animals for food
questions: Where do polar bears live?
What color is a polar bear's skin?
What do polar bears hunt?

cards.title: African Elephant
read: The African elephant is the biggest animal that lives on land. It lives in Africa, in grasslands and forests.

An elephant's trunk is its nose and upper lip together. It uses its trunk to smell, drink, eat, lift things and say hello. Elephants live in family groups called herds. An older female usually leads the herd.

Elephants greet each other by twisting their trunks together. They talk with low rumbles that other elephants can feel through the ground. Baby elephants drink milk and stay close to their mothers for years.
facts: A big elephant can weigh as much as three or four cars.
Its trunk has thousands of muscles.
Big ears help it cool off.
It can eat more than 300 pounds of plants a day.
Elephants use their tusks to dig and to lift things.
words: an elephant's long nose and upper lip
a group of animals that live together
a long tooth that grows out of the mouth
questions: Where do African elephants live?
Name two things an elephant does with its trunk.
Who leads the herd?

cards.title: Marie Curie
read: Marie Curie was born in 1867 in Warsaw, Poland. As a girl she loved to read and learn. Back then, women could not go to the university in Warsaw, so she moved to Paris, France, to study.

Marie became a scientist. With her husband, Pierre, she studied rocks that gave off a strange, invisible energy. She named this energy radioactivity, and she found two new elements called polonium and radium.
Marie worked very hard in her lab, often late into the night. She won two Nobel Prizes, one of the biggest awards in science. Her daughter Irène grew up to win a Nobel Prize too.
facts: She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
She is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, physics and chemistry.
She named polonium after Poland, the country where she was born.
She was the first woman to teach at her university in Paris.
She taught people to use X-ray machines so doctors could see broken bones.
words: a person who studies the world to learn how it works
one of the basic building blocks that everything is made of
a kind of invisible energy that comes from some materials
questions: Where was Marie Curie born?
What two new elements did she find?
How many Nobel Prizes did she win?

cards.title: Wangari Maathai
read: Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in Kenya, a country in Africa. As a girl she helped on her family's farm. She loved the big fig trees and clear streams near her home.

Wangari studied science in the United States and Germany, then came home to Kenya. She saw that many trees had been cut down, and women had to walk far for firewood and clean water. In 1977 she started the Green Belt Movement to plant trees.

Wangari taught women how to plant and care for tree seedlings. The trees gave them firewood, food and shade, and their roots helped hold the soil in place. Her idea spread to other countries in Africa and beyond.
facts: The Green Belt Movement has planted more than 50 million trees.
In 2004 she won the Nobel Peace Prize.
She was the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
She was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn the highest college degree, called a doctorate.
She liked to tell a story about a little hummingbird that does the best it can to help.
words: a group of people working together to make a change
questions: In what country was Wangari Maathai born?
What did she start in 1977?
How do tree roots help the land?

cards.title: Katherine Johnson
read: Katherine Johnson was born in 1918 in West Virginia. She loved to count everything: steps, dishes and even silverware. She was so good at math that she started high school at age 10.
Katherine worked at NASA, the group that sends people into space. She did math to figure out the exact path a spaceship should fly. Her work helped astronauts get to space and come home safely.
In 1962, astronaut John Glenn was getting ready to circle Earth. Computers had worked out his path, but he asked for Katherine to check the numbers first. She did, and his trip was a success.
facts: She helped plan the path for the first American in space, Alan Shepard, in 1961.
Her math helped Apollo 11 reach the Moon in 1969.
In 2015 she was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
A NASA building is named after her.
She lived to be 101 years old.
words: working with numbers, shapes and patterns
the way something moves from one place to another
a person trained to travel in space
questions: What did Katherine Johnson love to count?
What did John Glenn ask her to do?
Where did her math help Apollo 11 go?

cards.title: Mary Anning
read: Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a town by the sea in England. The cliffs there are full of fossils. As a child she hunted for fossils on the beach with her family.
When Mary was about 12, she and her brother found the skeleton of a huge sea reptile. It was called an ichthyosaur, which means fish lizard. It had lived long, long before there were any people.

Storms and landslides uncovered new fossils in the cliffs, so Mary searched after bad weather. She found the first full skeleton of another sea reptile, the plesiosaur. Scientists came from far away to learn from her.
facts: She sold fossils in her family's shop to help earn money.
In 1828 she found a pterosaur, a flying reptile.
Her dog, Tray, went with her on fossil hunts.
Some of her fossils are in the Natural History Museum in London.
People still find fossils on the beaches at Lyme Regis today.
words: what is left of a plant or animal from long ago, kept in rock
an animal with dry, scaly skin, like a lizard
all the bones of a body
questions: Where did Mary Anning hunt for fossils?
What did she and her brother find when she was about 12?
What was her dog's name?

cards.title: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
read: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in 1756 in Salzburg, a city in what is now Austria. His father was a music teacher. Little Wolfgang listened to his big sister, Nannerl, play the keyboard and wanted to play too.
Wolfgang learned fast. He wrote his first short pieces of music when he was about 5 years old. As children, he and Nannerl traveled across Europe to play for kings, queens and crowds.
When he grew up, Mozart wrote music for orchestras, pianos, singers and more. He wrote more than 600 pieces of music. People all over the world still play and love his music today.
facts: He played the keyboard and the violin.
He wrote his first symphony when he was about 8.
He wrote many operas.
One of his famous operas is The Magic Flute.
The house where he was born in Salzburg is now a museum.
words: a big group of musicians who play together
a long piece of music for an orchestra
a play where the actors sing the story
questions: Where was Mozart born?
About how old was he when he wrote his first pieces of music?
Name two instruments he played.

cards.title: Pelé
read: Pelé was born in 1940 in Brazil. His real name was Edson Arantes do Nascimento. His family did not have much money, so as a boy he practiced soccer with a sock stuffed with paper or rags.
Pelé practiced and practiced. At 17, he played for Brazil in the World Cup and helped his team win. He scored goals with his feet, his head and amazing moves.
Pelé played soccer for about 20 years. Later he played in New York and helped many Americans fall in love with soccer. He was known around the world for his big smile and his kindness to fans.
facts: He is the only player to win the World Cup three times.
He scored more than 1,000 goals, counting all kinds of games.
For most of his career, he played for a team in Brazil called Santos.
In Brazil, soccer is called futebol.
His nickname was The King.
words: a point scored by getting the ball into the net
a big soccer contest between teams from many countries
doing something again and again to get better
questions: In what country was Pelé born?
What did he use as a ball when he was a boy?
How many times did he win the World Cup?

cards.title: Ibn Battuta
read: Ibn Battuta was born in 1304 in Tangier, a city in Morocco, in North Africa. When he was 21, he set out on the hajj, the Muslim trip to Mecca, a holy city in Arabia. He did not come home for about 24 years!

Ibn Battuta traveled by camel, by horse, by boat and on foot. He visited places in Africa, the Middle East, India and Asia, and he said he even reached China. Along the way he met kings, traders and everyday families.

After he came home, he went on more trips, even across the Sahara to the land of Mali. Then he told the story of all his travels to a writer. The book, called the Rihla, still helps us learn what the world was like long ago.
facts: He traveled about 75,000 miles in his life.
He visited lands that are now more than 40 countries.
He worked as a judge in India and in the Maldives.
Rihla means journey.
His travels took about 30 years in all.
words: a person who buys and sells things
questions: In what city was Ibn Battuta born?
Name two ways he traveled.
What is the name of his book?

cards.title: Louis Braille
read: Louis Braille was born in 1809 in a small town in France. When he was 3, he hurt his eye in his father's workshop. By age 5 he was blind in both eyes, which means he could not see.
Louis went to a special school in Paris for blind children. The school had only a few books, with big raised letters that were hard to read by touch. Louis wanted a better way.

When he was only 15, Louis made a code of raised dots. Each letter is made of up to six dots that you feel with your fingertips. Today blind people all over the world read with this code, called braille.
facts: Each braille letter fits in a space with room for six dots.
Braille can show numbers and music too.
Louis grew up to be a teacher at his school.
You can find braille on elevator buttons and signs.
Braille is used for many languages.
words: a set of signs that stand for letters or words
sticking up so you can feel it
questions: How old was Louis when he made his code?
How many dots can each letter have?
Where can you find braille today?

cards.title: Katsushika Hokusai
read: Katsushika Hokusai was born in 1760 in Edo, the city now called Tokyo, in Japan. He started drawing when he was about 6 years old. He kept drawing for the rest of his long life.

Hokusai made pictures called woodblock prints. An artist drew a picture, and carvers cut it into blocks of wood. Then printers put ink on the blocks and pressed paper on top, so they could make many copies.
His most famous print is The Great Wave. It shows a giant wave curling over small boats, with Mount Fuji far behind. He made it when he was about 70 years old.
facts: He made about 30,000 pictures in his life.
The Great Wave is part of a set called Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.
He used more than 30 different artist names.
He filled books with sketches of people, animals and plants.
He lived to be about 88 years old.
words: a person who makes art, like drawings or paintings
a picture made by pressing ink onto paper
a person who cuts shapes into wood or stone
questions: What is the city of Edo called today?
What is Hokusai's most famous print?
How did printers make copies of a picture?

cards.title: Mount Everest
read: Mount Everest is the tallest mountain on Earth, measured from the level of the sea. It is in the Himalaya mountains, on the border of Nepal and China. Its top pokes up above many clouds.

The air at the top is very cold and thin, so climbers often carry tanks of oxygen to help them breathe. In 1953, Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary became the first people known to reach the summit, the very top.

The Sherpa people live in the valleys below Everest. Many Sherpa guides are expert climbers who help others reach the top. In Nepal the mountain is called Sagarmatha, and in Tibet it is called Chomolungma.
facts: It is about 29,032 feet tall, which is more than 5 miles high.
Its rocks hold fossils of sea animals from long ago.
Strong winds blow across the top much of the year.
The Himalaya mountains are still growing taller, very slowly.
Tenzing Norgay was a Sherpa.
words: the very top of a mountain
the part of the air we need to breathe
a line where one country ends and another begins
questions: Which two countries is Mount Everest between?
Who first reached the top in 1953?
Why do climbers carry oxygen?

cards.title: The Great Wall of China
read: The Great Wall of China is a very long wall that stretches across northern China. It winds over mountains, hills, deserts and grasslands.
People built and rebuilt walls here for more than 2,000 years to protect their land. Workers used dirt, stone, wood and bricks. Much of the wall people visit today was built about 500 years ago.
Guards watched from tall towers along the wall. To send a message fast, they could light fires or make smoke signals from tower to tower. Today millions of visitors come to walk along it.
facts: With all its parts, it is more than 13,000 miles long.
You cannot see it from the Moon with just your eyes.
Some parts are wide enough for horses to ride along the top.
Some very old parts have crumbled away.
Its name in Chinese means the Long Wall.
words: a sign that sends a message
questions: What country is the Great Wall in?
What did workers use to build it?
How did guards send messages fast?

cards.title: The Sahara Desert
read: The Sahara is the biggest hot desert in the world. It covers much of North Africa. A desert is a place that gets very little rain.
Some parts of the Sahara have tall hills of sand called dunes. But most of it is rocky land, gravel and mountains. Days can be very hot, and nights can get cold.

Plants and animals in the Sahara have special ways to live with little water. Fennec foxes have big ears that help them stay cool. People cross the desert with camels, and some families move from place to place with their animals.
facts: It is about as big as the United States.
Some sand dunes are more than 500 feet tall.
An oasis is a green spot in the desert where there is water.
Thousands of years ago, much of the Sahara was green, with lakes and grasslands.
Antarctica is a bigger desert, but it is a cold one.
words: a dry place that gets very little rain
a hill of sand made by the wind
a green spot with water in a desert
questions: On which continent is the Sahara?
What is a dune?
How do fennec foxes stay cool?

cards.title: The Nile River
read: The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world. It flows north through Africa and ends in the Mediterranean Sea. Its water comes from rain and lakes far to the south.
Most of Egypt is desert, but the land beside the Nile is green. Long ago, the river flooded every summer and left rich mud on the fields. Farmers grew wheat and other crops in this good soil.
People in ancient Egypt built cities and pyramids near the Nile. They sailed boats up and down it to carry food and stone. Today, millions of people still use the river for water, farming and travel.
facts: It is about 4,100 miles long.
The Nile and the rivers that feed it flow through about 11 countries.
Its two main branches are the White Nile and the Blue Nile.
The two branches meet in the city of Khartoum, in Sudan.
Crocodiles and hippos live along parts of the Nile.
words: when water spills over onto land that is usually dry
a plant that farmers grow for food
from a very long time ago
questions: Which way does the Nile flow?
What did the floods leave on the fields?
What are the Nile's two main branches?

cards.title: The Statue of Liberty
read: The Statue of Liberty stands on an island in New York Harbor. She holds a torch high in her right hand. In her left arm she holds a tablet with the date July 4, 1776, the birthday of the United States.
The statue was a gift from the people of France to the people of the United States. A French artist named Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi designed it. It was finished in 1886.

The statue is made of copper, which was once shiny brown like a penny. Over many years, air and water turned the copper green. For many people arriving by ship, it was one of the first things they saw in America.
facts: From her heel to the top of her torch, she is about 151 feet tall.
Her crown has 7 rays.
Her crown has 25 windows.
Gustave Eiffel, who built the Eiffel Tower, designed the metal frame inside.
Liberty means being free.
words: a stick with a light or fire at the top

cards.title: The Eiffel Tower
read: The Eiffel Tower is a tall iron tower in Paris, France. It was built for a big world's fair in 1889. Gustave Eiffel's company designed and built it.
Many people did not like the tower at first. They thought it looked strange. Now it is one of the most loved buildings in the world, and millions of people visit every year.
Visitors can ride elevators or climb stairs to go up. From the top, you can see far across Paris. At night, thousands of lights make the tower sparkle.

cards.title: Machu Picchu
read: Machu Picchu is an old stone city high in the Andes Mountains of Peru, in South America. The Inca people built it more than 500 years ago. Quechua people, who are descendants of the Inca, still live in the Andes today.
The Inca were amazing builders. They cut stones so carefully that the stones fit together without any mortar. Some walls are so tight that a knife blade cannot slide between the stones.

On the steep hillsides, the Inca made flat steps of land called terraces. The terraces helped them grow food and kept the soil from washing away. Today, visitors explore the ruins, and llamas sometimes wander by.
facts: It sits about 8,000 feet above the sea.

cards.title: The Galápagos Islands
read: The Galápagos Islands are a group of islands in the Pacific Ocean. They belong to Ecuador, a country in South America. The islands were made by volcanoes.

Many animals on the Galápagos live nowhere else on Earth. Giant tortoises munch on cactus, and marine iguanas swim in the sea to eat seaweed. Blue-footed boobies are birds that show off their bright blue feet.

In 1835, a young scientist named Charles Darwin visited the islands. He collected finches that had different beaks on different islands. Later, they helped him think about how living things change over a very long time.
facts: The islands are about 600 miles from the coast of South America.
Giant tortoises can live more than 100 years.

the hard mouth of a bird

cards.title: Uluru
read: Uluru is a giant red rock in the middle of Australia. It rises high above the flat, dry land around it. It is one of the biggest single rocks in the world.

Uluru is very special to the Anangu, an Aboriginal people, the traditional owners of this land. Their families have lived here for many thousands of years. Their stories, called Tjukurpa, teach how the land was made and how to care for it.
The rock seems to change color during the day. At sunrise and sunset it can glow bright orange and red. After rain, waterfalls pour down its sides, and small pools fill with water.
facts: It is about 1,142 feet tall.
Its red color comes from iron in the rock that has rusted.
Anangu and park rangers look after the park together.

cards.title: The Sun
read: The Sun is a star, a giant ball of hot, glowing gas. It is the closest star to Earth. It looks small only because it is very far away.
The Sun gives Earth light and heat. Plants use sunlight to make their food, and animals eat the plants. Without the Sun, Earth would be dark and frozen.
Earth spins like a top. When our side faces the Sun, it is day. When our side turns away, it is night. Earth also travels all the way around the Sun once a year.
facts: The Sun is about 93 million miles away.
More than a million Earths could fit inside it.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.

cards.title: Clouds
read: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water or bits of ice in the air. The drops are so small and light that they float.

When the Sun warms water in lakes and oceans, some of it turns into a gas you cannot see, called water vapor. The vapor rises and cools high in the sky. Then it turns back into tiny drops, and a cloud forms.
Inside a cloud, the drops bump together and grow bigger and heavier. When they get too heavy, they fall as rain. If the air is cold enough, they fall as snow.
facts: Puffy white clouds are called cumulus clouds.
Thin, wispy clouds high in the sky are called cirrus clouds. They are made of ice.
Dark gray clouds often bring rain.
Fog is a cloud that is down near the ground.

cards.title: Magnets
read: A magnet can pull some metals toward it without even touching them. It pulls things made of iron and steel, like paper clips and nails.
Every magnet has two ends, called poles: a north pole and a south pole. Two different poles pull together. Two poles that are the same push each other apart.
Earth itself acts like a giant magnet. A compass has a tiny magnet needle that points north, so it helps people find their way. Magnets are also inside speakers, toys and fridge doors.
facts: Magnets do not pull wood, plastic, paper or glass.

cards.title: Trees
read: Trees are the biggest plants on Earth. A tree has roots, a trunk, branches and leaves. The roots hold the tree in the ground and drink up water.
Leaves use sunlight, water and air to make food for the tree. As they do, they give off oxygen, the part of air that we need to breathe. Trees also give birds, squirrels and insects a home.
In many trees, the trunk grows a new layer of wood each year. If a tree is cut down, you can count the rings in the trunk to find out how old it was. Some trees live for thousands of years.
facts: The tallest trees, coast redwoods, can grow more than 350 feet tall.

cards.title: The Printing Press
read: Long ago in Europe, books were copied by hand, one letter at a time. It could take months to copy just one book, so books were rare.

Around 1450, a German man named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press. He made small metal letters that could be moved and lined up to spell words. The letters were inked, and the press squeezed paper down on top.
Now many copies could be made quickly. Books became cheaper, and more people learned to read. Ideas and news could spread farther and faster than ever before.
facts: Gutenberg's most famous book is the Gutenberg Bible, printed in the 1450s.
People in China and Korea printed with blocks and movable letters even earlier.

cards.title: Snowflakes
read: Snowflakes form high up in cold clouds. A tiny bit of water vapor freezes onto a speck of dust. More water freezes onto it, and it grows into an ice crystal.
Most snowflakes have six sides or six arms. As a snowflake falls, it passes through air that is colder, warmer, wetter or drier. Each change makes its arms grow in a different way.

In 1885, a farmer named Wilson Bentley took the first photo of a single snowflake, using a camera with a microscope. He took more than 5,000 snowflake pictures in his life. People called him Snowflake Bentley.
facts: Snow looks white because it bounces back all the colors of light.
Fresh snow soaks up sound, so a snowy day can seem very quiet.

Who took the first photo of a single snowflake?

cards.title: Lightning and Thunder
read: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity in the sky. Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice bump and rub together. This builds up electricity until it jumps across the sky or down to the ground.
Lightning is very hot. It heats the air so fast that the air bursts outward with a boom. That sound is thunder.
Light travels much faster than sound, so you see lightning before you hear thunder. Count the seconds between the flash and the boom. If you count 5 seconds, the storm is about one mile away.
facts: Lightning is hotter than the outside of the Sun.

cards.title: Shadows
read: A shadow is a dark shape that forms when something blocks light. Light travels in straight lines. When your body blocks the sunlight, a shadow shows up on the ground.
Shadows change during the day. In the morning and evening, when the Sun is low, shadows are long. Around noon, when the Sun is high in the sky, shadows are short.

Long ago, people used shadows to tell time. A sundial has a pointer that makes a shadow, and the shadow moves as the Sun moves across the sky. You can also make shadow puppets with your hands and a flashlight.
facts: Your shadow is always on the side away from the light.

cards.title: Giraffe
read: Giraffes are the tallest animals in the world. They live in Africa, in grasslands and open woodlands called savannas.
A giraffe's long neck helps it reach leaves high in trees. It wraps its long, dark tongue around branches to pull off leaves, even from thorny acacia trees. Giraffes spend most of their day eating.
Every giraffe has its own pattern of spots, like a fingerprint. A baby giraffe, called a calf, can stand up within about an hour of being born. Giraffes sleep only a little at a time.
facts: A giraffe's neck has 7 bones, the same number as yours.

cards.title: Kangaroo
read: Kangaroos live in Australia. They hop on their strong back legs and use their long tail for balance. They live in groups called mobs.
A kangaroo is a marsupial. That means the mother carries her baby in a pouch on her belly. A newborn baby, called a joey, is about the size of a jelly bean. It grows safely in the pouch for months.
Kangaroos eat grass and other plants. They rest in the shade during the hot day and come out to eat when it is cooler. To cool off, they lick their arms.
facts: A big red kangaroo can jump up to 25 feet in one hop.

cards.title: Blue Whale
read: The blue whale is the biggest animal that has ever lived, even bigger than the biggest dinosaurs. It lives in oceans all around the world.

Even though it is huge, a blue whale eats tiny animals called krill. It gulps a giant mouthful of water and krill. Then it pushes the water out through bristly plates called baleen, which trap the krill like a strainer.
A blue whale is a mammal, so it breathes air. It swims up to the surface and breathes out through blowholes on top of its head. The spray from its breath can shoot about 30 feet into the air.

cards.title: Giant Panda

Pandas eat mostly bamboo, a tall, woody grass. Bamboo does not give them much energy, so they eat for many hours a day. A panda has a special bump on its wrist that works like a thumb to help hold the bamboo.
A newborn panda cub is pink, tiny and almost hairless. It is about the size of a stick of butter. Its mother holds it close and keeps it warm.

cards.title: Monarch Butterfly
read: Monarch butterflies have bright orange wings with black lines and white spots. Their bright colors warn birds that they taste bad.
A monarch starts life as a tiny egg on a milkweed plant. A caterpillar hatches and eats milkweed leaves. Then it makes a hard, green case called a chrysalis, and inside, it changes into a butterfly.

Every fall, many monarchs from the United States and Canada migrate, or fly south, to Mexico. Millions of them rest together on fir trees in the mountains there. In spring they start the trip north, and their young finish it.

cards.title: Camel
read: Camels are built for life in the desert. A dromedary camel has one hump, and a Bactrian camel has two.
A camel's hump does not hold water. It holds fat, which the camel's body can use for energy when food is hard to find. A thirsty camel can drink more than 30 gallons of water in about 13 minutes.

Camels have long eyelashes, and they can close their nostrils to keep out blowing sand. Their wide, flat feet help them walk on soft sand without sinking. People have used camels for thousands of years to carry loads and give milk.

cards.title: Cheetah

A cheetah's body is made for speed. It has long, thin legs, a light body and a bendy back. Its long tail helps it balance and turn while it runs.

Cheetahs live mostly in the grasslands of Africa. They hunt in the daytime, using their sharp eyes to spot animals like gazelles. Black lines called tear marks run from their eyes to their mouths and may help block the glare of the sun.

Many bats sleep during the day, hanging upside down in caves, trees or buildings. They wake up at night to find food. Most bats eat insects, and some eat fruit or drink nectar from flowers.
Many bats find their way in the dark using echolocation. A bat makes high squeaks and listens for the echoes that bounce back. The echoes tell the bat where bugs and trees are.

cards.title: George Washington Carver
read: George Washington Carver was born around 1864 in Missouri. He was born enslaved, but slavery soon ended. As a boy he cared for plants and helped sick ones grow. People called him the Plant Doctor.

cards.title: Sacagawea
read: Sacagawea was a Lemhi Shoshone girl. She was born around 1788 in what is now Idaho. When she was about 12, she was captured in a raid by another tribe. She was taken far from her family.

How many waterfalls make up Niagara Falls?
What can you see in the mist on sunny days?

cards.title: Pyramids of Giza
read: The Pyramids of Giza stand in the desert near Cairo, the capital of Egypt. They were built about 4,500 years ago. The three big ones were made as tombs for kings called pharaohs.

The biggest is the Great Pyramid. It was built for a pharaoh named Khufu. Workers used more than 2 million heavy stone blocks. They moved and stacked them with ropes, sleds, ramps and lots of teamwork.
Near the pyramids sits the Great Sphinx. It is a giant statue with the body of a lion and the head of a person. People come from all over the world to see these wonders.
facts: For about 3,800 years, the Great Pyramid was the tallest building made by people.
It was once covered in smooth, shiny white stone.
It is the only Wonder of the Ancient World still standing.
The workers lived in a town near the pyramids.
Giza has three big pyramids and some smaller ones.
words: a shape with a square bottom and triangle sides that meet at the top
a place where a person is buried
questions: In what country are the Pyramids of Giza?
Who were the pyramids built for?
What animal's body does the Great Sphinx have?

cards.title: Venice
read: Venice is a city in Italy. It is built on more than 100 small islands in a shallow lagoon by the sea. In Venice, many streets are made of water. They are called canals.
There are no cars on the streets of old Venice. People walk over bridges or ride in boats. Buses are boats, and even ambulances and fire trucks are boats! The biggest canal is the Grand Canal.
Long ago, builders pushed wooden poles deep into the mud. Then they built houses, churches and palaces on top. Many of those buildings have stood for hundreds of years.
facts: Venice has about 400 bridges.
A gondola is a long, thin boat. Most gondolas are painted black.
A gondolier stands up and rows with one long oar.
Sometimes high tides flood the city's squares.
Venice is famous for colorful glass made on the island of Murano.
words: a waterway made or shaped by people
shallow water partly cut off from the sea
a long, narrow boat used in Venice
questions: What country is Venice in?
How do people get around in Venice?
What did builders push into the mud long ago?

cards.title: The Arctic
read: The Arctic is the cold land and sea around the North Pole, at the top of the world. In the middle is the Arctic Ocean. Much of it is covered by a thick layer of floating sea ice.
In summer the sun stays up all day and all night. In winter the sun may not rise for weeks. Polar bears, Arctic foxes, walruses and caribou live in the Arctic.
People have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years. The Inuit, the Sámi and many other Indigenous peoples call it home. They know the land, sea and ice well. Today many live in towns and cities.
facts: There is no land at the North Pole, only ice floating on the ocean.
Eight countries have land in the Arctic.
Wild penguins do not live in the Arctic.
Most Arctic foxes grow white fur for winter.
A narwhal is an Arctic whale with a long tusk.
words: the most northern point on Earth
the first peoples of a place, and their families today
questions: What is in the middle of the Arctic?
What happens to the sun in the Arctic summer?
Name two animals that live in the Arctic.

cards.title: The Wheel
read: Long ago, people had to carry heavy loads or drag them on the ground. About 5,500 years ago, people made one of the best inventions ever: the wheel. Some of the first wheels spun clay to make pots.
Later, people put wheels on carts. A wheel needs an axle, a rod through its middle. The axle holds the wheel on while it turns. Wheels made it much easier to move heavy things.
The first wheels were solid wood. Later, people made wheels with spokes, which were lighter and faster. Today wheels are everywhere: on bikes, cars, trains, toys and even shopping carts.
facts: One of the oldest wooden wheels ever found is more than 5,000 years old.
It was found in a marsh in Slovenia, a country in Europe.
A wheel rolls instead of scraping, so things move more easily.
Gears are wheels with teeth that help machines work.
A Ferris wheel is a giant wheel you can ride.
words: a rod that a wheel turns on
a bar from the middle of a wheel to its edge
something new that someone makes for the first time
questions: About how long ago did people make the first wheels?
What is an axle?
Name three things that have wheels.

cards.title: Rockets
read: A rocket is a machine that can fly into space. It burns fuel, which makes lots of hot gas. The gas blasts out the bottom of the rocket. As the gas pushes down, the rocket is pushed up!
People in China made the first rockets about 800 years ago. They were a lot like fireworks. In 1926 Robert Goddard, an American scientist, launched the first rocket that used liquid fuel.
Today big rockets carry astronauts, satellites and space robots into space. The Saturn V rocket carried astronauts to the Moon. It was about as tall as a 36-story building.
facts: To circle Earth, a rocket must go about 17,500 miles per hour.
Rockets carry their own oxygen, so they can burn fuel in space.
Goddard's first liquid-fuel rocket flew about 41 feet high.
That flight lasted only about 2 and a half seconds.
Let go of a blown-up balloon and the air pushes it like a rocket.
words: to send something up into the air or space
a machine that goes around Earth in space
questions: What pushes a rocket up?
Where were the first rockets made?
Which rocket carried astronauts to the Moon?

cards.title: Trains
read: A train is a line of cars pulled along a track by an engine called a locomotive. Trains carry people and goods from place to place. Steel wheels roll on steel rails, so trains can pull very heavy loads.

The first steam trains for the public ran about 200 years ago in England. Fire heated water to make steam. The steam pushed parts that turned the wheels. Steam trains puffed smoke and blew loud whistles.

In 1869 workers, many from China, finished the first railroad across the United States. Trips that took months now took about a week. Today the fastest trains in Japan, China and France go about 200 miles per hour.
facts: A train track has two rails.
A golden spike marked the end of the railroad in 1869.
Japan's bullet trains began running in 1964.
Maglev trains use magnets to float above the track.
Some freight trains are more than a mile long.
words: the engine that pulls a train
a long steel bar that train wheels roll on
goods carried by a train, truck, ship or plane
questions: What is the engine of a train called?
What made steam trains go?
What do maglev trains use to float?

cards.title: Dinosaurs
read: Dinosaurs were reptiles that lived on Earth for millions of years, long before people. Some were as big as a building. Some were as small as a chicken. Some ate plants, and some ate meat.
About 66 million years ago, a giant space rock crashed into Earth. The world changed, and the big dinosaurs died out. But not all dinosaurs! Birds are living dinosaurs.
We know about dinosaurs from fossils. Fossils are bones, teeth, eggs and footprints saved in rock for a very long time. Scientists who dig up and study fossils are called paleontologists.
facts: The word dinosaur means "terrible lizard."
Dinosaur fossils have been found on every continent, even Antarctica.
Tyrannosaurus rex had teeth about as long as bananas.
No person ever saw a living T. rex.
Some dinosaurs had feathers.
words: a sign of a very old living thing saved in rock
an animal with scaly skin, like a lizard or snake
questions: About when did the big dinosaurs die out?
What animals alive today are dinosaurs?
How do we know about dinosaurs?

cards.title: Maps
read: A map is a drawing of a place, as if you were a bird looking down from the sky. Maps can show a room, a town, a country or the whole world. They help us find our way.
Many maps have helpers. A map key, or legend, tells what the little pictures and colors mean. A compass rose shows the directions north, south, east and west.
People have made maps for thousands of years. One of the oldest world maps is on a clay tablet from Babylon, in what is now Iraq. Today, pictures taken from space help people make very exact maps.
facts: Most maps put north at the top.
A globe is a map shaped like a ball, just like Earth.
On many maps, blue means water.
A person who makes maps is called a cartographer.
You can draw a map of your own bedroom!
words: a box that tells what the pictures on a map mean
a symbol that shows north, south, east and west
questions: What does a map key tell you?
What are the four directions on a compass rose?
What is a globe?

cards.title: The Ocean
read: The ocean is a huge body of salty water. It covers about 7 out of every 10 parts of Earth's surface. From space, Earth looks like a big blue marble.
All the ocean water is connected, but people give it five names. They are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic Oceans. The Pacific is the biggest and deepest of all.
The ocean is home to whales, fish, crabs, coral and tiny living things called plankton. Some plankton make much of the oxygen we breathe. Wind blowing across the water makes waves.
facts: The deepest place in the ocean is almost 7 miles deep.
It is called the Challenger Deep.
Almost all of Earth's water is in the ocean.
Ocean water is too salty for people to drink.
People have not yet explored most of the ocean.
words: a huge body of salty water
tiny living things that drift in water
a gas in the air that people and animals need to breathe
questions: How many named oceans are there?
Which ocean is the biggest?
What makes waves?

cards.title: Emperor Penguin
read: Emperor penguins are the biggest penguins in the world. A grown-up can be about as tall as a first grader. They live in Antarctica, one of the coldest places on Earth.
Emperor penguins cannot fly. Their wings work like flippers to help them swim. They dive deep into the icy sea to catch fish, squid and krill. Thick feathers and fat keep them warm.
In winter, a mother lays one egg. The father holds it on his feet, under a warm flap of skin, for about two months. He does not eat that whole time! The fathers huddle together to stay warm.
facts: They can dive more than 500 meters, or 1,600 feet, deep.
They can hold their breath for more than 20 minutes.
Chicks are covered in fluffy gray feathers called down.
Penguins sometimes slide across the ice on their bellies.
Each penguin has its own call, so its family can find it.
words: a flat body part used for swimming
tiny shrimp-like animals that live in the sea
questions: Where do emperor penguins live?
What do their wings help them do?
Who keeps the egg warm?

cards.title: Sea Turtle
read: Sea turtles live in oceans all around the world. They have flippers instead of feet, so they are strong swimmers. Unlike many land turtles, they cannot pull their heads into their shells.
A mother sea turtle swims back to the beach where she hatched, or one close by. At night, she digs a hole in the sand and lays about 100 eggs. Then she covers them up and goes back to the sea.
About two months later, the babies hatch. They are called hatchlings. They dig out of the sand, often at night, and crawl toward the bright water. Then they swim out to sea to begin their lives.
facts: There are seven kinds of sea turtles.
The leatherback is the biggest. It can weigh more than 1,000 pounds.
Warm sand makes more girl turtles. Cooler sand makes more boys.
Green sea turtles eat seagrass and algae.
Sea turtles have lived on Earth for more than 100 million years.
words: a flat body part used for swimming
to come out of an egg
a baby animal that just came out of its egg
questions: What do sea turtles have instead of feet?
Where does a mother sea turtle lay her eggs?
What do baby turtles do after they hatch?

cards.title: Gray Wolf
read: Gray wolves are the biggest wild members of the dog family. They live in forests, mountains, grasslands and snowy places in North America, Europe and Asia. Their thick fur can be gray, brown, black or white.
Wolves live in family groups called packs. A pack is usually a mother, a father and their young. The pack hunts together, plays together and takes care of the pups.
Wolves howl to talk to each other. A howl can tell the pack where a wolf is or warn other wolves to stay away. Pups are born in a den. At first they cannot see or hear.
facts: Pet dogs are relatives of wolves.
A wolf can eat about 20 pounds of meat in one meal.
A wolf's howl can be heard miles away.
Wolves were brought back to Yellowstone National Park in 1995.
Wolves have a very strong sense of smell.
words: a safe hole or cave where some animals rest and raise babies
questions: What is a family group of wolves called?
Why do wolves howl?
Where are wolf pups born?

cards.title: Owls
read: Owls are birds that are great hunters. There are more than 200 kinds of owls. They live on every continent except Antarctica. Most owls are nocturnal, which means they hunt at night.
Owls have big eyes that face forward. Their eyes cannot move around, so an owl turns its whole head instead. It can turn its head about three-quarters of the way around!
Owls fly almost without a sound. Soft, fringed feathers on their wings quiet the air. Owls also hear very well. Some can find a mouse under the snow just by listening.
facts: The elf owl is about as big as a sparrow.
Owls often swallow small prey whole.
Later they cough up a pellet of bones and fur.
A barn owl's ears are at different heights, which helps it find sounds.
Snowy owls hunt in the daytime.
words: a small ball of bones and fur that an owl coughs up
an animal that is hunted for food
questions: Why does an owl turn its whole head?
How do owls fly so quietly?
What is in an owl pellet?

cards.title: Frogs
read: Frogs are amphibians. That means they live part of their lives in water and part on land. Frogs live on every continent except Antarctica. There are more than 7,000 kinds.
A frog starts life as a tiny egg in the water. The egg hatches into a tadpole, which has a tail and breathes with gills. Slowly it grows legs, loses its tail and becomes a frog.
Frogs do not drink water with their mouths. They soak it in through their skin. Many frogs catch bugs with long, sticky tongues. Strong back legs help them jump far and swim fast.
facts: Frogs use their eyes to help them swallow.
The goliath frog is the biggest frog. It can grow about as long as a ruler.
Bright colors on poison dart frogs warn, "Do not eat me!"
Wood frogs can freeze in winter and thaw out in spring.
A group of frogs is sometimes called an army.
words: an animal that lives part of its life in water and part on land
a baby frog that lives in water
body parts that let an animal breathe under water
questions: What is a baby frog called?
How do frogs drink water?
What helps frogs jump far?

cards.title: Ants
read: Ants are insects. Like all insects, they have six legs and three body parts. They use the two antennae on their heads to smell, touch and talk to each other.
Ants live together in big groups called colonies. Each colony has at least one queen who lays eggs. Worker ants build the nest, find food and care for the young. Some colonies have millions of ants.
Ants talk with smells. When an ant finds food, it leaves a smelly trail on its way home. Other ants follow the trail to the food. That is why you often see ants marching in a line.
facts: Ants can carry things many times heavier than their own bodies.
There are more than 12,000 kinds of ants.
Ants live on every continent except Antarctica.
Leafcutter ants grow gardens of fungus to eat.
Worker ants are all girls.
words: a small animal with six legs and three body parts
a big group of animals that live together
questions: How many legs does an ant have?
Who lays the eggs in an ant colony?
How do ants show each other where food is?

cards.title: Tiger
read: Tigers are the biggest wild cats in the world. They live in forests, grasslands and swamps in Asia. Each tiger has its own pattern of stripes. No two tigers have the same stripes.

Unlike most cats, tigers love water. They are strong swimmers and often cool off in rivers and pools. Tigers usually live and hunt alone. They hunt mostly at night and sneak up quietly on prey like deer and wild pigs.
A mother tiger has two to four cubs at a time. The cubs are born blind. They stay with their mother for about two years while she teaches them how to hunt.
facts: A tiger's skin is striped too, not just its fur.
The Siberian tiger, also called the Amur tiger, is one of the biggest kinds.
A tiger's roar can be heard far away, maybe up to 2 miles.
Stripes help tigers hide in tall grass and shadows.
Only a few thousand tigers live in the wild, and people work to protect them.
words: a long, thin line of color
a baby tiger, lion, bear or panda
an animal that is hunted for food
questions: Where do wild tigers live?
How are tigers different from most cats?
How long do cubs stay with their mother?
